newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BT seeks new German telecom partner.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BT seeks new German telecom partner.

text.p: British Telecommunications (BT) said on Wednesday it was in talks with potential partners to give it fresh infrastructure or equity after German utility RWE quit its alliance with the British group and Germany's Viag.

BT dismissed RWE's move to join Germany's Veba AG and BT's main British rival Cable & Wireless as a mere "hiccup" in its plans to compete against giant Deutsche Telekom when the German market is deregulated in 1998.

News that RWE was in advanced talks to switch telecom partners comes as BT prepares to bid with Viag for Germany's fourth mobile telephone licence -- the digital DCS 1800 megahertz mobile network licence, dubbed E2.

"We're going alone (with Viag) for the fourth mobile licence in Germany -- but obviously we'll need some additional partners -- maybe on the infrastructure side or maybe on the equity side (in the longer term)," a company spokesman told Reuters.
Analysts were little surprised at RWE's decision to drop its former partners, noting that there had been rumours that the German energy giant had been talking to other venture partners.
"From a BT pespective, RWE's withdrawal is more of an irritation than a disaster," said Laurence Heyworth, telecoms analyst at Robert Fleming Securities.
"Given BT's strength and financial resources, there's no question that BT is perfectly capable of addressing the German market alone and/or in conjunction with another partner."

SG Strauss Turnbull's John Tysoe said BT's share of the cost of winning Germany's new mobile phone licence had jumped to 2.5 billion marks ($1.63 billion) as its stake in the joint venture with Viag increased from 37.5 percent to 50 percent.
"But what's that between friends?" Tysoe asked. "It's going to be a little bit more expensive for them but it all comes out in the wash."
"The phone world is not going to deregulate gloablly again. this opportunity that exists now won't be there in the future. Unless you buy into it now, you've lost your chance."
Some analysts tipped German steel and engineering group Thyssen AG, which has service expertise and existing network operations, as a possible new partner.
But BT declined to indentify potential alliances. "We talk to each other all the time, so when things start to go a bit wonky, you just step up the old calls," the spokesman said.
BT said it was still interested in RWE's northern German fixed telecom links, adding that it was still hoping to negotiate access to its local infrastructure.

"If you're building a mobile network, you still need the fixed links between all the bases. RWE did have northern German fixed links and we are still carrying on talking to them," the spokesman said. But he added: "There are other infrastucture providers around."
BT said that relations with RWE had soured because of divergent views of the importance of mobile telecommunications in the liberalising German markets.

"Do you believe that mobile is the way the world is going, or do you believe it will stay fixed?...BT and Viag believe in fixed/mobile integration and RWE didn't," the spokesman said. "RWE also wanted to build much more infrastructure than BT did."
BT said its German joint venture Viag Interkom, which serves about 300 large business customers, would continue to be the basis for developing a full telecom service provider in Germany.
Cable and Wireless said it planned to make a statement later on Wednesday. ($1=1.5297 Mark)
